questions.lessonTitle: Effect of Length Penalties on Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, Composer 2 adds a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The penalty formula uses hyperparameters k and q which define the curvature, and the input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.

questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Regularization in Composer 2 RL Training
questions.lessonContent: Similar to prior work, Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularization, calculated as KL(q||p) = Ex~q[-log r(x)] where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source implementations estimate KL with the k3 estimator, which is an unbiased estimator that reduces variance when p and q are close. However, the content notes that Amini et al. showed the variance increases drastically as p and q diverge, and for large KL values the variance of the k3 estimate is extremely large. Since the k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased, Composer 2 instead uses the standard estimator k1 = -log r.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use to avoid variance blow-up in RL training?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Composer 2 uses the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead of k3, because k3 variance increases drastically as p and q diverge for large KL values.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. Since agent rollouts can be very long, especially for long-horizon coherency, maintaining stability is critical. The main strategy to minimize off-policy sample divergence involves fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, similar to PipelineRL. Inference workers can update weights mid-rollout, meaning later tokens in a rollout are less off-policy. To further reduce divergence between sampling and training policies, the system replays MoE routing to ensure consistent expert selection between inference and training forward passes.

questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator Usage in Composer 2 Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator for Kullback-Leibler divergence regularization instead of the k3 estimator. The k3 estimator is unbiased and reduces variance when the policies are close, but research shows that its variance increases drastically as the policies diverge. For large KL values, the variance of the k3 estimate becomes extremely large. Since this variance blow-up could cause training instability, the training team opted for the standard k1 estimator which is more stable despite potentially being slightly biased.

However, Amini et al. shows in [6, Figure 1] that the variance increases drastically as p and q diverge... Therefore, we use the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead.' This confirms the statement is true.

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Token Prediction Layer Training in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 trains additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers to enable faster inference through speculative decoding. These MTP layers are initialized from scratch rather than from a pre-trained checkpoint. To accelerate their convergence, the model uses self-distillation, teaching the MTP layers to predict the exact logit distribution of the main language model head at each position. The MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run, and during the final two phases of continued pretraining (long-context extension and SFT), the MTP layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.

questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty Formula in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests. The formula is: Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1 - q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining the curvature of the penalty. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
